title: Why the U.S. Navy Cannot Clear the Mines in the Strait of Hormuz
fullText: The United States Navy just spent 39 days dismantling the entire Iranian Navy. Over 120 warships destroyed. Every submarine sunk. Billions of dollars in military hardware turned to scrap metal at the bottom of the Persian Gulf. And yet right now, as of today, more than 600 ships are sitting outside the straight of Hormuz going nowhere. Not because Iran has warships blocking the way. Not because there are fighter jets stopping them, because of objects the size of a trash can sitting on the seafloor, naval mines, weapons that cost less than a used car. And here is the part that almost nobody is talking about. The United States Navy does not currently have the equipment to clear them. The four dedicated mine clearing ships that were stationed in the region for over 30 years were pulled out and retired 6 months before this war started. Their replacements have never been tested in combat, and the timeline for clearing the straight, according to defense officials, stretches to late summer at the earliest. By the end of this video, you will fully understand why the most expensive navy ever built cannot solve a problem created by some of the cheapest weapons ever made, and why even Iran itself may not be able to fix what it started. Let us start with what a naval mine actually is. Because most people hear the word mine and picture something from a World War II movie, a metal ball with spikes floating in the water waiting for a ship to bump into it. That image is not entirely wrong, but it is dangerously incomplete. Modern naval mines come in three types, and each one kills ships in a completely different way. The first type is the contact mine. This is the closest to what you picture from old war movies. A metal shell filled with explosives anchored to the seafloor by a cable floating just below the surface. When a ship's hull touches it, the mine explodes. Simple, cheap, and effective. Iran has thousands of these. They cost somewhere between $1,000 and $5,000 each. You could buy one for the price of a decent laptop. The second type is the influence mine. This one sits on the bottom of the sea and waits. It does not need to be touched. Instead, it listens. It has sensors that detect the magnetic field of a steel ship passing overhead or the sound of a propeller or the pressure wave that a large hull pushes through the water. When the right combination of signals matches what the mine is looking for, it detonates from below. Think of it like a motion sensor light on your front porch, except instead of turning on a light, it fires an explosion upward through the water into the bottom of the ship. The ship does not even need to be close. Some influence mines can detect a vessel from over a 100 meters away and still deliver a lethal blast. The third type is the one that terrifies naval commanders the most. The rocket propelled rising mine. This weapon sits on the seafloor completely silent, completely invisible. It listens for a propeller. When it hears the right sound, it does not just explode in place. It launches a warhead upward through the water at 260 ft pers. The warhead travels from the bottom of the sea to the hull of the ship in less than 2 seconds. The ship's crew does not hear a warning. There is no alarm. There is no time to react. The first sign that something is wrong is a hole in the bottom of the hull and seawater flooding the engine room. This is not a theoretical weapon. Iran has hundreds of them. Now, here is where it gets really interesting. In 1988, a single Iranian mine, one mine that cost roughly $1,500, hit the American frigate USS Samuel B. Roberts in the Persian Gulf. That one mine ripped a 15 ft hole in the hull, cracked the ship's keel, flooded two engine rooms, and injured 10 sailors. The ship did not sink, but it came close. It took 13 months and $89.5 million to repair. One mine, $1,500, $89 million to fix the damage. That is a cost ratio of almost 60,000 to1 in favor of the mine. Now take that math and multiply it by the number of mines Iran has available. Estimates range from 2,000 to 6,000. Even at the low end, the numbers are staggering. But here is the problem. Knowing that mines are in the water is not the same as being able to get them out. And this is where the story of the Strait of Hormuz turns from a military victory into something much more complicated. For over 30 years, the United States kept four Avenger class mine sweepers permanently stationed in Bahrain right next to the Strait. These ships were purpose-built for one job, finding and destroying mines. Their holes were made of wood and fiberglass, not steel, so they would not trigger magnetic mines. They moved slowly and deliberately through the water, towing sonar equipment that could map the seafloor and identify objects sitting on the bottom. They carried specially trained divers who would do something most people cannot even imagine. These divers would put on wet suits, drop into water where they know an explosive device is sitting on the bottom, swim down to it, physically attach a small explosive charge to the mine's casing, swim back to what they hoped was a safe distance, and trigger the detonation underwater in near zero visibility with currents pushing them around, knowing that one wrong move, one bump against the wrong sensor, and the mine goes off while they are next to it. They did this one mine at a time. It was the most dangerous job in the Navy, but it worked. Those four ships were the only dedicated mine clearing capability the United States had in the entire Middle East. In September 2025, 5 months before the first Tomahawk missile hit Iran, the Navy pulled all four ships out of Bahrain and sent them to Philadelphia to be scrapped. 30 years of mine clearing expertise loaded onto a transport ship and sent home to be cut apart for recycling. The reason, according to the Navy, was that the ships were old and expensive to maintain. Some of them had been in service for over 30 years. The wood in their hulls needed constant care. Their engines were outdated, keeping them operational cost millions per year. Their replacements, the Navy said, were coming. Newer ships, better technology, faster results. That was the promise. The replacements were literal combat ships, a class of warship that the Navy had spent over $30 billion developing. The idea was simple. Instead of having one ship that only clears mines, build a ship that can swap between different missions by loading different equipment packages. Need to hunt submarines. Load the submarine package. Need to clear mines. Load the mine package. It sounds logical on paper. The problem is that the mine clearing package has never been proven to work. The Pentagon's own testing office reported that they could not determine whether the system was effective because there was not enough data. The underwater drone that is supposed to find mines on the seafloor has trouble identifying them even in calm, clear water off the coast of California. The system that is supposed to destroy the mines after they are found was rated not operationally suitable with equipment working less than 30% of the time. And unlike the old Avenger ships where the mine clearing gear was built into the ship and ready to go, every single piece of equipment on the new ships has to be individually lowered into the water, connected, calibrated, and monitored. A process that takes hours before a single mine can even be searched for. Imagine you hired a plumber to fix a leak, and before he could even look at the pipe, he had to spend 4 hours assembling his tools in your driveway. That is what the Navy is dealing with right now. The United States spent $30 billion building a replacement for four wooden ships. And right now, with thousands of mines potentially sitting in the most important waterway on Earth, the replacement cannot reliably do the job. There is another angle that almost nobody is talking about. Even if the equipment worked perfectly, the process of clearing mines is unbelievably slow. A mind sweeper moves through the water at roughly 5 knots, which is slower than most people jog. Each pass covers a strip about 100 to 200 meters wide. After each pass, the ship turns around and comes back to sweep the next strip. Think of it like mowing a lawn, except the lawn is 21 mi wide. You cannot see the grass, and some of the grass might kill you if you get too close. The straight of Hormuz is approximately 35 m long and 21 m wide at its narrowest point. The actual shipping lanes are narrower, roughly 6 m, but mines do not care about shipping lanes. They go wherever the current takes them. An influence mine laid in one spot can drift hundreds of meters before settling again. A contact mine on a long cable can swing in wide arcs with the tide. So even after you clear a lane, the lane might not stay clear. Iran understands this math better than anyone. They know that laying a mine takes minutes. A small boat pulls up to a spot, rolls the mine over the side, and drives away. Clearing that same mine can take days. One crew working carefully to avoid detonating the weapon they are trying to remove, spending hours on a single object. At that rate, if Iran laid even a few hundred mines across the straight, clearing them could take months. Clearing mines is harder than clearing land mines on land. And landmine clearance is already one of the most dangerous jobs on Earth. With sea mines, you are working in three dimensions instead of two. The mine might be on the surface in the middle of the water or on the bottom. And there is a fourth problem that landmines do not have. Time. Ocean currents move things. A mine you cleared from one area can drift back into it. A lane you swept yesterday might not be safe today. The ocean does not stay still, and neither do the mines. And that is exactly what has happened. On March 10th, American intelligence confirmed that Iran had begun laying mines in the straight of Hormuz. The types detected included the Mahan 3, a 300 kg mine with acoustic sensors, and the Maham 7, a 220 kg bottom mine that can be dropped from small boats or helicopters. And this is the part of the story where we need to stop for a moment because something happened recently that changes the entire picture. On April 9th, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy did something unprecedented. They published a map, a navigational chart showing the Strait of Hormuz with the established international shipping lanes marked as a danger zone. This was the first time Iran officially admitted that it had placed mines in the waterway. But the map did more than just confirm what everyone already suspected. It told the world exactly what Iran is now doing with the Strait. The map directed all commercial ships away from the normal shipping lanes and into a narrow 5mm corridor near Laric Island. To use this corridor, every ship must submit its identification number, a full list of the crew, a complete cargo description, the ownership history of the vessel, and the final destination. All to contacts linked to the Revolutionary Guard. Then the ship receives a radio code that functions as a transit permit. Without the code, you do not pass. Iran did not offer to reopen the strait of Hormuz. Iran offered to manage it on its own terms indefinitely. And then came the toll. Iran's parliament passed something called the Straight of Hormuz Management Plan on March 30th. Under this plan, every ship passing through the straight must pay $1 per barrel of oil on board. payment accepted in Bitcoin or stable coin cryptocurrency, not US dollars. For a standard oil tanker carrying 2 million barrels, that is a $2 million fee to pass through a waterway that has been free for all of recorded history. Some ships have reportedly been charged in Chinese yuan instead. Think about what that means. Iran lost its entire navy. Its supreme leader is dead. Its military infrastructure is shattered and it is now running a toll booth on the most important shipping lane on the planet. Collecting fees in cryptocurrency that American sanctions cannot touch. Channeling global oil traffic through a corridor it controls and demanding paperwork that gives it a complete intelligence picture of every ship, every crew and every cargo passing through. The ceasefire assumed Iran would simply reopen the strait. Iran is doing something far more strategic. It is keeping the straight technically open but functionally under its control. 5 to seven ships per day are getting through. The normal number is over 130. That is not an open waterway. That is a choke point being operated as a business. Now, here is where this starts affecting people who have never heard of the straight of Hormuz and do not care about naval mines. If you live in the United States, you have already noticed gas prices have climbed to $410 per gallon, up 37% since February 28th. Diesel is even higher. Every truck that delivers food to your grocery store runs on diesel. Every cargo ship that brings products to American ports burns fuel that is priced against global oil markets. Oil is sitting above $19 per barrel right now. Before the war, it was below 70. The daily cost of the Hormuz's closure to the global economy is estimated at $3.2 billion. Not per month, per day. That number goes directly into the price of everything you buy. Your groceries, your gas, your heating bill, the cost of anything that was shipped by truck or boat, which is essentially everything. And it gets worse. Iran's foreign minister recently said that reopening the straight would happen with, and this is his exact phrase, due consideration of technical limitations. American officials believe that phrase is a polite way of saying something extraordinary. Iran may not know where all of its own mines are. According to reporting from the New York Times, US officials say Iran may not have accurate records of every mine it laid. Some mines were deployed in a scattered and disorganized manner. Others have likely drifted from their original positions due to currents. The weapons Iran put in the water to close the straight may now be impossible for Iran itself to fully account for. The country that laid the mines cannot guarantee where they all are. And the country that wants to clear them does not have the equipment to do it quickly. This is where the conversation fundamentally changes. The United States asked NATO allies this week to deliver written plans for securing the Strait of Hormuz within days. The problem is that NATO is in the same situation. Most NATO countries retired their mind sweepers years ago. The few that remain are small, old, and designed for the shallow waters of the North Sea and the Baltic, not the deep, warm, current, heavy waters of the Persian Gulf. Japan has mind sweepers. South Korea has some, but those ships are stationed in the Pacific and would take weeks to redeploy. The four remaining American Avenger class ships are in SEBO, Japan. thousands of miles away. The situation is almost absurd when you step back and look at it. The United States has two aircraft carriers in the region, the Lincoln and the Ford. It has dozens of destroyers, cruisers, and submarines. It has hundreds of fighter jets. It has satellites that can read a license plate from orbit. And none of it matters against a weapon that costs less than a month's rent in most American cities, sitting silently on the bottom of the ocean, waiting. Meanwhile, the mines sit on the seafloor of the Strait of Hormuz, patient, silent, waiting for a propeller, a magnetic field, or a steel hull passing overhead. They do not care about ceasefires. They do not expire. They do not negotiate. They just wait. You just heard how the most powerful navy on Earth destroyed every warship Iran ever built and still cannot reopen a 21-m wide shipping lane. The weapons that closed the straight cost less than most family cars. The ships designed to clear those weapons were sent to a scrapyard 5 months before the war started. The replacements do not work reliably. And Iran itself may have lost track of where it planted them. The ceasefire is holding, but the strait is not open. 600 ships are waiting. Oil prices are climbing. And somewhere on the bottom of the Persian Gulf, a $1,500 mine is listening for the sound of a propeller. So, here is the question. The United States retired its mine clearing ships to save money on maintenance. Those ships cost a fraction of what a single destroyer costs to operate. Now the entire global economy is losing $3.2 billion per day because the strait cannot be cleared. Was retiring those ships a smart budget decision or was it the most expensive costcutting mistake in military history? Write your answer in the comments because the people who say budget priorities and the people who say strategic disaster are about to have a very important argument under this video. And if you have not seen our video on how the United States destroyed Iran's entire navy in 39 days and why it still was not enough to reopen the straight, make sure to watch that one text.
